---
title: "Predicting observations the model did not see"
---

The [linear-regression checks](../regression-models/checking-linear-regression.qmd) assessed how a fitted model reproduces the observations used to estimate it. Predictive evaluation asks a different question about responses that did not contribute to fitting.

Suppose a regression predicts reading time from word length, frequency, and contextual predictability. Its fitted residuals are small. This tells us how closely the fitted predictions track the responses used to estimate the model. It does not tell us how well the procedure predicts a response unavailable during fitting.

We must also say whether the omitted response comes from an observed passage, an omitted passage, an observed reader, or an omitted reader. A fitted description does not answer this question on its own.

## Four decisions precede a score

A predictive evaluation makes four linked decisions.

1. The statement of [what must be held out](prediction-targets.qmd) identifies which observations or groups are absent during fitting and what information is available about them.
2. The [loss function](predictive-loss.qmd) determines how much each discrepancy between an observation and prediction costs.
3. The training and evaluation split ensures that the responses used for evaluation did not guide fitting or model choice.
4. The evaluation unit returns predictive differences to the speakers, items, passages, or languages represented by the claim.

These decisions cannot be made independently. If a complete passage must be absent during fitting, word positions from that passage must move together into the test set. If passage sizes differ, a position-weighted loss and a passage-weighted loss answer different questions. Uncertainty over predictive improvement should not treat arbitrary computational folds as independent passages.

## Three ways to hold out observations

Consider a corpus with 20 readers, 10 passages, and 100 word positions per passage. The same regression procedure may be evaluated with at least three data separations.

| predictive question | what is omitted during fitting | what the result may describe |
|:--|:--|:--|
| another trial | one observed response | another response from represented readers and passages |
| a new reader | every response from one reader | responses from readers absent during fitting |
| a new passage | every position in one passage | responses from passages absent during fitting |

A random row split can evaluate the first question because other trials from the same readers and passages may remain in training. It cannot evaluate the second or third question, since the supposedly omitted group is partly observed during fitting.

This is why a report that one model *predicts better* is incomplete. Better for which response, under which loss, and with which observations or groups excluded from fitting?

## Use predictive comparison to test a theoretical contrast

The point of held-out prediction is not to generate a leaderboard of formulas. Predictive evaluation can test a theoretically motivated contrast. A control model may encode design and lexical variables. A second model may add full-form predictability. A third may add graded syntactic and semantic predictability. Each addition corresponds to a linguistic claim.

The held-out comparison asks whether that added information changes prediction for the specified observations. A coefficient and a predictive improvement answer related but distinct questions. The coefficient describes an estimated conditional association in the fitted model. The loss comparison describes the consequence of adding that information for responses excluded from fitting.

A model may fit on average while failing for long passages, rare words, one response range, or particular speakers. Retaining pointwise and groupwise losses allows us to locate such failures rather than hiding them inside one aggregate number.

## How the module proceeds

We begin with [what must be new at prediction time](prediction-targets.qmd), which distinguishes an omitted trial from an omitted participant, item, passage, or language. [Predictive loss](predictive-loss.qmd) then defines the numerical consequence assigned to each error. [Prediction bias and prediction variance](bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd) explain why closer training fit need not imply lower error on new responses.

Next, [training and test data](training-and-test-data.qmd) enforce the separation between fitting and evaluation. [Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd) rotates that separation so that every observation receives a held-out prediction. [Leave-one-out cross-validation](leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd) uses one observation as the test set at a time. [Grouped cross-validation](grouped-cross-validation.qmd) keeps complete speakers, items, passages, or languages together whenever those groups must be absent during fitting.

We then turn to comparisons. [Comparing predictive loss](comparing-predictive-loss.qmd) evaluates two procedures on the same held-out observations and shows why uncertainty should be summarized at the level specified by the scientific claim. [Likelihood-ratio tests](likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd) compare nested likelihood models in sample, and [information criteria](information-criteria.qmd) penalize in-sample fit. Finally, [PSIS-LOO](psis-loo.qmd) approximates leave-one-out prediction from posterior draws, while [WAIC](waic.qmd) constructs a separate posterior-variance correction from the same pointwise log-likelihood matrix.

## The assessment connection

[PS2](../assignments/index.qmd) applies the predictive sequence to reading-time data. It asks whether lexical, morphosyntactic, and semantic predictability measures improve prediction for passages omitted during fitting. Complete passages are held out, so the split, loss aggregation, and interpretation must all remain at the passage level.

The assessment is included here because it turns an underspecified predictive question into an analysis decision. A random row split would evaluate other positions from represented passages even if every printed score were computed correctly.

## What this module adds

By the end of the module, we should be able to state what a predictive score estimates, reconstruct how each prediction was kept out of its own fit, and identify the units over which model differences vary. These capabilities let us replace the vague claim that a model predicts well with a narrower claim whose response, loss, and held-out observations are explicit.
